chapter.title: Vendor Lock
chapter.sub: One integrator's password opens 740 devices. Fourteen people know it. The booking panels depend on it too.

items.text: SEASON 7 · EPISODE 6 · DRAFT · CASE-039  Security audit · Maya, Mara, Oskar and Adaeze · Level L5 · Advanced support (formulas on request)  Seven hundred and forty devices, one integrator’s password, fourteen people who know it — and a booking system that breaks if you change it.  ⚑ RV-153: governance, not technique — security owns access. RV-151: figures illustrative. Some choices run on a clock.

items.title: Vendor Lock
items.stakes: One integrator's password opens 740 devices. Fourteen people know it. Changing it will break every booking panel.
items.reward: One guarded door, keys Corvane owns, and panels that still show Monday's meetings.

objectives.text: Find who can reach the doors
Put management behind one guarded door

items.rumor: Seven hundred and forty doors. One key. Fourteen people holding it.

items.alt: The operations centre; Mara points at an audit summary on the wall; Maya reads.

bubbles.text: Same password on every device Ferrant ever touched. Since 2019.

items.caption: Seven hundred and forty.

lines.text: Same password on every device Ferrant ever touched. Since 2019.
Then before anyone changes anything, I want to know everything that uses it.

items.text: ✦ UX RULE #67 · AVERY'S LENS  Credentials belong to the owner, not the installer  Whoever holds the keys holds the system. The organisation that owns the rooms must own every credential, configuration and way in.  One integrator's password opened 740 devices in 31 sites. Corvane couldn't change it without the integrator — or without breaking its own booking panels.

items.alt: An access sheet: one red USERS VLAN box holding staff laptops, Ferrant's VPN pool and 740 management logins; below: one password, fourteen people, four have left; 64% of the estate; the booking integration's 740 scripts.
items.caption: One key, and everyone standing at the door.

items.prompt: 10:00. Mara wants a plan by Friday. What do you do first?
items.risk: A key that can't be taken back, on most of the estate.
timeout: The week fills with other audits.
Friday's review gets a finding and no plan.

hints.text: Before any key changes: who holds it, who can reach the lock, what else turns it?

options.label: Change the password on all 740 devices tonight
options.result: You don't yet know what else logs in with it.
options.fail: Find what depends on a key before you change it.

options.label: Find out who knows it, what can reach the logins, and everything that logs in with it — then take Mara the whole picture so she can decide the order
options.result: By Wednesday: fourteen people, a user VLAN wide open, and 740 scripts nobody had mentioned.
options.consequence: Reach, holders and dependencies, for the person who owns access.

options.label: Disable Ferrant's VPN account yourself, now
options.result: Mara: “That's my decision — and I'll make it with facts, today.”

options.label: It's been fine since 2019 — leave it
options.consequence: Accepting a risk that isn't yours.

items.title: One key, forty doors.
items.body: Fourteen people at Ferrant know the password; four have left the company. And the password isn't the only problem: the devices' management ports sit on the user VLAN, where Ferrant's remote-support VPN also lands. Anyone on the staff network — or holding that VPN — can reach a login page on 740 devices.
items.label: Test: how far has the key travelled — and who can reach the doors?

items.sub: Advanced · the skill behind this chapter

items.alt: A teaching moment: Mara and Maya beside a board. Seven hundred and forty of our eleven hundred and fifty devices — sixty-four percent — on one password fourteen people know. What first? Who can reach them. If only the jump host reaches management, that password stops being a door for everyone else. Then we rotate, site by site. Reach first, then keys. I own the vault. You own not breaking the booking panels.

items.label: **Fix it:** put device management behind one guarded door.

items.text: Act II — “The password in the schedules”

items.title: The password in the schedules.
items.body: Adaeze finds it: the room-booking integration logs into every control processor as admin, with the shared password, from 740 scheduled scripts — to read one calendar field. Change the password tonight, and on Monday every booking panel in the estate is blank.
items.label: Test: what happens if you rotate tonight — and what should the integration use?

items.prompt: Wednesday. How do the keys change?
unknown: Whether the service account works everywhere
items.risk: Blank booking panels estate-wide — or a key that never changes.
timeout: The password stays as it was since 2019.

hints.text: What shrinks the risk today, and what must exist before the key can change?

options.label: Rotate tonight anyway and fix the panels on Monday
options.result: Monday: 600 rooms with blank panels and a queue at every desk.
options.consequence: The estate pays for the order of operations.

options.label: Reach first this week — MGMT VLAN and jump host by the network team, approved by Mara. Then a least-privilege service account for the integration from Mara's vault, tested on one site. Then unique credentials site by site, pilot first
options.result: Thursday: the door is guarded. Next week: the pilot site's bookings still show and the old password is rejected. The rest follow at four sites a week.
options.consequence: Reach, then keys — without a blank panel.

options.label: Leave the password — rotation is too risky
options.result: Mara: “That's a risk acceptance. It's mine to make, and I won't.”

options.label: Give every Corvane engineer the password too, so Ferrant isn't the only holder
options.consequence: Spreads the key instead of changing the lock.

items.title: The password file that printed itself
items.body: At MIT in the mid-1960s, one of the first computers to use passwords — the Compatible Time-Sharing System — once greeted every user at login with the entire password file, after two people's editing jobs collided and the files swapped. A single shared file had become everyone's secret. The fix then is the fix now: fewer people with the keys, and changes you can trace.

items.alt: The access sheet after the change: three boxes — USERS with staff laptops, MGMT with 740 logins, VENDOR with Ferrant's VPN — and a jump host between MGMT and VENDOR with named logins and recorded sessions; the integration on a service account from the vault; unique credentials per site, pilot first.
items.caption: One door, guarded. Keys that can be taken back.

items.prompt: Look — one password meant we could fix any room in five minutes. Your people loved that.

options.label: “They did. And we'll keep fast support — through the jump host, with your own named logins. Your people, our keys.”
options.reply: …Named logins. Fine. My auditors will like that more than I do.

options.label: “Four of the people who know it don't work for you any more, Oskar.”
options.reply: …Yes. I know. I've been trying not to think about it.

options.label: “You've locked us in.”
options.reply: You never asked for the keys.

items.title: CORVANE-ALL
items.body: A spreadsheet on Ferrant's file share, last edited 2019: one row, ‘CORVANE-ALL’, and the password. Shared with a team list of fourteen. Four of the names no longer resolve to anyone.

items.prompt: Next month. What does the Ferrant contract say from now on?
timeout: The next site is built with a shared password.

hints.text: Who should own the keys — and how do you leave a supplier if you must?

options.label: Switch integrators
options.result: The next integrator sets its own shared password.

options.label: Corvane owns every credential and configuration; Ferrant staff get named accounts through the jump host; configurations are handed over after each visit; an exit plan is tested once a year
options.result: Oskar signs, and asks to use the clauses with his other clients.
options.consequence: Owners own the keys; installers get named, revocable access.

options.label: Trust Oskar
options.result: Oskar is trustworthy. His ex-staff are four unknowns.

options.label: Do everything in-house from now on
options.result: No budget, no team, forty sites.

items.title: admin
items.body: The room-booking integration's script, copied 740 times: ‘login as admin, password from config’. It needs to read one calendar field. It logs in with the power to reconfigure the room.

items.alt: Valmera's new training centre rack room: heat shimmer over one rack's lower units, marked off by a dashed outline. Luis, on the phone, stands well back.

bubbles.text: The new rack room smells of hot varnish. Nobody's touching anything. The electrician's on her way.
Good. Keep everyone back — I'm calling in now.

items.text: FIELD NOTE —  One password on most of an estate is one leak from everything, with no way to revoke one person. Fix reach first — management on its own VLAN behind a jump host with named, recorded logins — then find everything that uses the key, give each a least-privilege account from security’s vault, and rotate site by site. The owner owns the keys; installers get named, revocable access. Access decisions are security’s.
